messages.content: Inspired by the provided input: Generate a complete, linear model with variables, objective function and constraints. The MILP should be described completely with equations and assumptions. The input is inspiration, so keep close to it, if you can and if information is missing, make reasonable assumptions and mark them as such. Do not ask questions. Use the following approach for your task: Use the or_operator to generate an MILP based on your input. Review the MILP and feedback improvements to the or_operator and let it try again. Just return the final model.

Based on your input, generate a complete, linear model with variables, objective function and constraints.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

Below is a **complete linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** for the problem described in the prompt.  
The model integrates  

* **train‑rescheduling** (choice of which side of a partially blocked segment a train uses, and the order in which trains that share the same side pass the segment), and  
* **speed‑management** (selection of a discrete speed level on each free segment, which determines travel time and energy consumption).

All symbols, sets, parameters and decision variables are defined first, then the objective function, followed by a list of linear constraints.  Wherever a product of a binary variable and a continuous variable appears (e.g. `o_{i,j}·τ_{t,seg}`) a standard big‑M linearisation is used, so the whole model is a **MILP**.

---

## 1.  Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** | Set of trains, indexed by *t* |
| **S** | Set of sides of a blocked segment, `S = {L,R}` (left / right) |
| **B** | Set of **blocked** track segments (the segment that is partially closed) |
| **F** | Set of **free** track segments (all other segments) |
| **N_t** | Ordered set of stations visited by train *t* (including the entry and exit of every segment) |
| **Seg(t,n)** | Segment travelled by train *t* when it departs station *n* and arrives at the next station.  For a blocked segment the segment belongs to **B**, otherwise to **F**. |
| **P** | Set of ordered train pairs that share at least one common segment (i.e. could conflict).  Each element is a pair *(i,j)* with *i ≠ j*. |
| **L** | Set of admissible discrete speed levels, indexed by *ℓ* (e.g. ℓ = 1,…,L).  The actual speed value for level ℓ is `v̂_ℓ`. |

---

## 2.  Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Typical value / unit |
|--------|-------------|----------------------|
| `sched_arr_t` | Scheduled arrival time of train *t* at its final station (the “on‑time” reference) | minutes |
| `dwell_n` | Minimum dwell time at station *n* (same for all trains) | minutes |
| `len_seg` | Physical length of segment *seg* (km) | km |
| `v̂_ℓ` | Speed (km/min) associated with discrete level ℓ | km/min |
| `e_ℓ` | Energy consumption rate (kWh per minute) when travelling at speed level ℓ | kWh/min |
| `v_min , v_max` | Minimum / maximum admissible speed on any free segment (km/min) | km/min |
| `safety_gap` | Minimum temporal head‑way required between two trains on the same side (minutes) | minutes |
| `T_start , T_end` | Start / end of the disruption window during which the blocked side cannot be occupied (minutes) | minutes |
| `M_time` | A large enough time constant (big‑M) – e.g. the planning horizon (≥ max possible arrival time) | minutes |
| `M_ord` | A large enough ordering constant – e.g. `M_time` (used for ordering linearisation) | minutes |
| `w_delay` | Weight of total delay in the objective | – |
| `w_energy` | Weight of total energy consumption in the objective | – |
| `δ_{t,ℓ}` | Indicator: 1 if speed level ℓ is allowed for train *t* on a given segment (e.g. due to train‑type limits) | – |
| `bigM_c` | Large constant used to “turn off’’ a train when it is cancelled (≥ M_time) | minutes |

All big‑M constants are chosen **tight** but safely larger than any feasible value of the associated continuous variable (e.g. `M_time = planning horizon = 1440 min` for a 24‑h horizon).

---

## 3.  Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| `r_{t,s}` | binary | 1 if train *t* uses side *s* (L or R) of the blocked segment, 0 otherwise. |
| `o_{i,j}` | binary | 1 if train *i* passes the **shared** side **before** train *j* (i.e. *i* precedes *j*).  For any pair *(i,j)∈P* we also have `o_{j,i}=1‑o_{i,j}`. |
| `c_t` | binary | 1 if train *t* is **canceled** (i.e. removed from the schedule). |
| `a_{t,n}` | continuous ≥0 | Arrival time of train *t* at station *n*. |
| `d_{t,n}` | continuous ≥0 | Departure time of train *t* from station *n*. |
| `τ_{t,seg}` | continuous ≥0 | Travel time of train *t* on segment *seg*. |
| `x_{t,seg,ℓ}` | binary | 1 if train *t* travels on segment *seg* with speed level ℓ, 0 otherwise.  For each (t,seg) exactly one level is chosen (unless the train is cancelled). |
| `v_{t,seg}` | continuous ≥0 | Actual speed of train *t* on segment *seg* (km/min).  It will be forced to equal one of the discrete values `v̂_ℓ` through the `x`‑variables. |
| `e_{t,seg}` | continuous ≥0 | Energy consumption on segment *seg* (kWh).  Linearised as `e_{t,seg}= Σ_ℓ e_ℓ·x_{t,seg,ℓ}·τ_{t,seg}` (linearised with big‑M). |

---

## 4.  Linearisation of the product *binary × continuous*  

For any binary variable `z∈{0,1}` and continuous variable `y∈[0, Ymax]` we introduce an auxiliary continuous variable `w` that represents the product `z·y`:

```
w ≤  Ymax·z
w ≥  0
w ≤  y
w ≥  y – Ymax·(1‑z)
```

In the model we use this pattern for:

* `o_{i,j}·τ_{i,seg}` and `o_{i,j}·τ_{j,seg}` (ordering constraints) – with `Ymax = M_time`.
* `x_{t,seg,ℓ}·τ_{t,seg}` (energy term) – with `Ymax = M_time`.

All auxiliary variables are named `w_…` in the constraints below.

---

## 5.  Objective Function  

\[
\min \; 
\underbrace{w_{\text{delay}}\;\sum_{t\in T}\Bigl(a_{t,\text{last}}- \text{sched\_arr}_t\Bigr)}_{\text{total passenger delay}} 
\;+\;
\underbrace{w_{\text{energy}}\;\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{seg}\;e_{t,seg}}_{\text{total energy consumption}}
\]

*`a_{t,last}`* is the arrival time at the **final** station of train *t* (the last element of `N_t`).  
If a train is cancelled (`c_t = 1`) we force its contribution to the delay term to zero by adding a big‑M term (see constraint (13) below).

Both components are linear because `e_{t,seg}` has already been linearised.

---

## 6.  Constraints  

### 6.1  Side‑choice on the blocked segment  

For every train that traverses a blocked segment *b∈B* :

\[
\sum_{s\in S} r_{t,s}= 1 \qquad\forall t\in T\text{ that use }b
\tag{1}
\]

If a train does **not** use a blocked segment, the corresponding `r_{t,s}` variables are forced to 0 (or simply omitted).

### 6.2  Ordering on a common side  

Consider any ordered pair *(i,j)∈P* that share a **blocked** segment *b* **and** use the **same** side *s*.  
Let `seg_{i}` and `seg_{j}` be the (identical) blocked segment for the two trains.  
Define auxiliary variables  

* `w_{i,j}^{τ}`  = `o_{i,j}·τ_{i,seg}`  
* `w_{j,i}^{τ}`  = `o_{i,j}·τ_{j,seg}`  

Linearisation (big‑M = `M_time`) :

```
w_{i,j}^{τ} ≤ M_time·o_{i,j}
w_{i,j}^{τ} ≥ 0
w_{i,j}^{τ} ≤ τ_{i,seg}
w_{i,j}^{τ} ≥ τ_{i,seg} – M_time·(1‑o_{i,j})
```

(and analogously for `w_{j,i}^{τ}`).

The **head‑way** constraint becomes

\[
a_{j,\text{entry}} \;\ge\; d_{i,\text{exit}} \;+\; safety\_gap\; o_{i,j}
\qquad\forall (i,j)\in P,\; \text{if } r_{i,s}=r_{j,s}=1
\tag{2}
\]

Because the model is linear, we replace the conditional “if both use the same side’’ by a big‑M formulation:

```
a_{j,entry} ≥ d_{i,exit} + safety_gap – M_ord·(2 – r_{i,s} – r_{j,s})
```

If either train does not use side *s*, the right‑hand side is relaxed by the big‑M term.

### 6.3  No conflict when opposite sides are used  

If two trains use opposite sides of the blocked segment they can occupy it simultaneously, therefore no ordering constraint is needed.  The big‑M term in (2) automatically de‑activates the constraint when `r_{i,s}+r_{j,s}=1`.

### 6.4  Dwell‑time at stations  

\[
d_{t,n}= a_{t,n}+ dwell_{n}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; n\in N_t
\tag{3}
\]

If a train is cancelled (`c_t = 1`) we relax the equality with a big‑M:

\[
d_{t,n} \ge a_{t,n}+ dwell_{n} - bigM_c\;c_t
\qquad
d_{t,n} \le a_{t,n}+ dwell_{n} + bigM_c\;c_t
\tag{3‑c}
\]

### 6.5  Travel‑time linking arrival / departure  

For every segment *seg* that train *t* traverses (including blocked and free segments):

\[
a_{t,\,\text{next}(n)} = d_{t,n} + \tau_{t,seg}
\qquad\forall t,\; n\in N_t\text{ with } seg = Seg(t,n)
\tag{4}
\]

If the train is cancelled we again relax with `bigM_c·c_t`.

### 6.6  Travel time ↔ speed (free segments)  

For any **free** segment *seg∈F* :

\[
\tau_{t,seg}= \frac{len_{seg}}{v_{t,seg}}
\qquad\forall t\text{ that use }seg
\tag{5}
\]

Because `v_{t,seg}` is a discrete speed, we enforce it with the `x`‑variables:

\[
v_{t,seg}= \sum_{\ell\in L} \hat v_{\ell}\,x_{t,seg,\ell}
\qquad\forall t,seg\in F
\tag{5‑a}
\]

\[
\sum_{\ell\in L} x_{t,seg,\ell}= 1 - c_t \qquad\forall t,seg\in F
\tag{5‑b}
\]

If the train is cancelled (`c_t=1`) the sum forces all `x` to 0 and consequently `v_{t,seg}=0`, `τ_{t,seg}=0`.

### 6.7  Speed limits (free segments)  

\[
v_{\min}\;(1-c_t) \le v_{t,seg} \le v_{\max}\;(1-c_t)
\qquad\forall t,seg\in F
\tag{6}
\]

### 6.8  Ordering‑consistency for each pair  

For every pair *(i,j)∈P* :

\[
o_{i,j}+o_{j,i}=1 \qquad\forall (i,j)\in P
\tag{7}
\]

If the two trains never share a segment (e.g. they are on different routes) we can set `o_{i,j}=0` a priori, but the above equality is safe because the big‑M in (2) will make the constraint non‑binding.

### 6.9  Blocked‑side occupation window  

No train may occupy the blocked side **s\*** (the side that is actually closed) during the disruption interval `[T_start,T_end]`.  
Let `s*` be the side that is **unavailable** (e.g. the left side). For any train *t* that uses the blocked segment:

\[
a_{t,\text{entry}} \ge T_{end} \; \text{or}\; d_{t,\text{exit}} \le T_{start}
\]

Linearised with a binary “use‑blocked‑side’’ variable `b_t = r_{t,s*}` :

```
a_{t,entry} ≥ T_end – M_time·(1‑b_t)
d_{t,exit} ≤ T_start + M_time·(1‑b_t)
```

If `b_t = 0` (train does **not** use the closed side) the constraints are relaxed; if `b_t = 1` they force the train to be completely outside the window.

### 6.10  Cancellation effect on delay term  

To keep the objective linear we set the delay contribution of a cancelled train to zero:

\[
a_{t,\text{last}} - \text{sched\_arr}_t \le M_{time}\;c_t
\qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{10}
\]

Thus when `c_t = 1` the term can be at most `M_time` (which is later subtracted by the weight, effectively removing the train from the objective).

### 6.11  Domain restrictions  

\[
\begin{aligned}
& r_{t,s}\in\{0,1\},\; o_{i,j}\in\{0,1\},\; c_t\in\{0,1\},\; x_{t,seg,\ell}\in\{0,1\}\\
& a_{t,n}\ge 0,\; d_{t,n}\ge 0,\; \tau_{t,seg}\ge 0,\; v_{t,seg}\ge 0,\; e_{t,seg}\ge 0
\end{aligned}
\tag{11}
\]

---

## 7.  Full MILP Model (compact notation)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& w_{\text{delay}}\sum_{t\in T}\bigl(a_{t,\text{last}}-\text{sched\_arr}_t\bigr)
      + w_{\text{energy}}\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{seg}\;e_{t,seg} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{s\in S} r_{t,s}=1 &&\forall t\text{ using a blocked segment} \tag{1}\\
& a_{j,\text{entry}} \ge d_{i,\text{exit}}+safety\_gap
   -M_{ord}\bigl(2-r_{i,s}-r_{j,s}\bigr) &&\forall (i,j)\in P,\;s\in S \tag{2}\\
& d_{t,n}=a_{t,n}+dwell_n &&\forall t,n \tag{3}\\
& a_{t,\text{next}(n)} = d_{t,n}+ \tau_{t,Seg(t,n)} &&\forall t,n \tag{4}\\
& \tau_{t,seg}= \frac{len_{seg}}{v_{t,seg}} &&\forall t,seg\in F \tag{5}\\
& v_{t,seg}= \sum_{\ell\in L}\hat v_{\ell}\,x_{t,seg,\ell} &&\forall t,seg\in F \tag{5a}\\
& \sum_{\ell\in L} x_{t,seg,\ell}=1-c_t &&\forall t,seg\in F \tag{5b}\\
& v_{\min}(1-c_t)\le v_{t,seg}\le v_{\max}(1-c_t) &&\forall t,seg\in F \tag{6}\\
& o_{i,j}+o_{j,i}=1 &&\forall (i,j)\in P \tag{7}\\
& a_{t,\text{entry}} \ge T_{end} - M_{time}(1-r_{t,s*}) &&\forall t \tag{8a}\\
& d_{t,\text{exit}} \le T_{start}+ M_{time}(1-r_{t,s*}) &&\forall t \tag{8b}\\
& a_{t,\text{last}}-\text{sched\_arr}_t \le M_{time}\,c_t &&\forall t \tag{10}\\
& \text{Linearisation constraints for } w_{i,j}^{\tau},\; w_{j,i}^{\tau},
   \; e_{t,seg}= \sum_{\ell} e_{\ell}\,x_{t,seg,\ell}\,\tau_{t,seg} \tag{Lin}\\
& \text{Domain restrictions } (11)
\end{aligned}
\]

All auxiliary linearisation constraints (labelled **Lin**) are the standard four‑inequality set described in Section 4.

---

## 8.  How the model works  

* **Side choice** – Constraint (1) forces each train that meets the blocked segment to pick exactly one side.  
* **Ordering** – If two trains pick the same side, binary `o_{i,j}` decides who goes first; (2) guarantees a safety head‑way. The big‑M term de‑activates the constraint when the trains are on opposite sides.  
* **Timing** – (3)–(4) propagate arrivals, departures and travel times along the whole route.  
* **Speed & energy** – The discrete speed level is selected by the `x`‑variables; (5)–(6) link speed to travel time and enforce limits. Energy consumption is linearised as the product of the chosen speed‑level rate and the travel time.  
* **Disruption window** – (8) forces any train that uses the *closed* side to be completely outside the interval `[T_start,T_end]`.  
* **Cancellation** – Binary `c_t` allows the model to drop a train (e.g. when the disruption makes it impossible to keep it on time). The big‑M terms in (3‑c), (4‑c) and (10) switch off all timing constraints and the delay contribution for cancelled trains.  
* **Objective** – A weighted sum of total passenger delay and total energy use is minimised. By adjusting `w_delay` and `w_energy` the planner can give priority to punctuality or to energy efficiency.

---

### Ready‑to‑use

The formulation above is **purely linear** (all products have been replaced by auxiliary variables and big‑M constraints).  It can be entered directly into any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …) using a modelling language such as AMPL, GAMS, Pyomo, or JuMP.  The only data that must be supplied are the sets, parameters (segment lengths, speed levels, dwell times, disruption window, etc.) and the big‑M constants that are large enough for the planning horizon.  

Feel free to adapt the weighting coefficients, tighten the big‑M values, or add extra practical constraints (e.g., crew‑change windows, platform capacity) – the structure of the model will remain unchanged.

Please generate an MILP based on the provided description.

Formulate a MILP for integrated train rescheduling and speed management under partial segment blockage. Variables: binary route choice r_{t,s} (train t uses side s of segment), binary order o_{i,j} (train i precedes j on shared track), continuous arrival a_{t,n}, departure d_{t,n} at station n, travel time τ_{t,seg} on segment, speed level v_{t,seg} (discretized). Objective: minimize weighted sum of total delay Σ_t (a_{t,last}-scheduled_arrival_t) and energy consumption Σ_t Σ_seg e(v_{t,seg})·τ_{t,seg}. Constraints: (1) each train chooses exactly one side on blocked segment; (2) if both trains on same side, enforce ordering: a_j >= d_i + safety_gap * o_{i,j}; (3) if opposite sides, no conflict. (4) time feasibility: d_{t,n}=a_{t,n}+dwell_n. (5) travel time linked to speed: τ_{t,seg}=length_seg / v_{t,seg}. (6) speed limits: v_min ≤ v_{t,seg} ≤ v_max. (7) binary ordering consistency: o_{i,j}+o_{j,i}=1 for any pair sharing track. (8) disruption window: trains cannot occupy blocked side during [T_start,T_end]. (9) optional cancellation binary c_t with big-M on times. Provide all sets, parameters, and big-M values. Assume discretized speed levels L. Provide linearization for product o_{i,j}*τ etc using big-M. Return full model.

| `safety_gap` | Minimum temporal head‑way required between two trains on the same side (minutes) | minutes |
| `T_start , T_end` | Start / end of the disruption window during which the blocked side cannot be occupied (minutes) | minutes |
| `M_time` | A large enough time constant (big‑M) – e.g. the planning horizon (≥ max possible arrival time) | minutes |
| `M_ord` | A large enough ordering constant – e.g. `M_time` (used for ordering linearisation) | minutes |
| `w_delay` | Weight of total delay in the objective | – |
| `w_energy` | Weight of total energy consumption in the objective | – |
| `δ_{t,ℓ}` | Indicator: 1 if speed level ℓ is allowed for train *t* on a given segment (e.g. due to train‑type limits) | – |
| `bigM_c` | Large constant used to “turn off’’ a train when it is cancelled (≥ M_time) | minutes |

All big‑M constants are chosen **tight** but safely larger than any feasible value of the associated continuous variable (e.g. `M_time = planning horizon = 1440 min` for a 24‑h horizon).

---

## 3.  Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| `r_{t,s}` | binary | 1 if train *t* uses side *s* (L or R) of the blocked segment, 0 otherwise. |
| `o_{i,j}` | binary | 1 if train *i* passes the **shared** side **before** train *j* (i.e. *i* precedes *j*).  For any pair *(i,j)∈P* we also have `o_{j,i}=1‑o_{i,j}`. |
| `c_t` | binary | 1 if train *t* is **canceled** (i.e. removed from the schedule). |
| `a_{t,n}` | continuous ≥0 | Arrival time of train *t* at station *n*. |
| `d_{t,n}` | continuous ≥0 | Departure time of train *t* from station *n*. |
| `τ_{t,seg}` | continuous ≥0 | Travel time of train *t* on segment *seg*. |
| `x_{t,seg,ℓ}` | binary | 1 if train *t* travels on segment *seg* with speed level ℓ, 0 otherwise.  For each (t,seg) exactly one level is chosen (unless the train is cancelled). |
| `v_{t,seg}` | continuous ≥0 | Actual speed of train *t* on segment *seg* (km/min).  It will be forced to equal one of the discrete values `v̂_ℓ` through the `x`‑variables. |
| `e_{t,seg}` | continuous ≥0 | Energy consumption on segment *seg* (kWh).  Linearised as `e_{t,seg}= Σ_ℓ e_ℓ·x_{t,seg,ℓ}·τ_{t,seg}` (linearised with big‑M). |

---

## 4.  Linearisation of the product *binary × continuous*  

For any binary variable `z∈{0,1}` and continuous variable `y∈[0, Ymax]` we introduce an auxiliary continuous variable `w` that represents the product `z·y`:

```
w ≤  Ymax·z
w ≥  0
w ≤  y
w ≥  y – Ymax·(1‑z)
```

In the model we use this pattern for:

* `o_{i,j}·τ_{i,seg}` and `o_{i,j}·τ_{j,seg}` (ordering constraints) – with `Ymax = M_time`.
* `x_{t,seg,ℓ}·τ_{t,seg}` (energy term) – with `Ymax = M_time`.

All auxiliary variables are named `w_…` in the constraints below.

---

## 5.  Objective Function  

\[
\min \; 
\underbrace{w_{\text{delay}}\;\sum_{t\in T}\Bigl(a_{t,\text{last}}- \text{sched\_arr}_t\Bigr)}_{\text{total passenger delay}} 
\;+\;
\underbrace{w_{\text{energy}}\;\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{seg}\;e_{t,seg}}_{\text{total energy consumption}}
\]

*`a_{t,last}`* is the arrival time at the **final** station of train *t* (the last element of `N_t`).  
If a train is cancelled (`c_t = 1`) we force its contribution to the delay term to zero by adding a big‑M term (see constraint (13) below).

Both components are linear because `e_{t,seg}` has already been linearised.

---

## 6.  Constraints  

### 6.1  Side‑choice on the blocked segment  

For every train that traverses a blocked segment *b∈B* :

\[
\sum_{s\in S} r_{t,s}= 1 \qquad\forall t\in T\text{ that use }b
\tag{1}
\]

If a train does **not** use a blocked segment, the corresponding `r_{t,s}` variables are forced to 0 (or simply omitted).

### 6.2  Ordering on a common side  

Consider any ordered pair *(i,j)∈P* that share a **blocked** segment *b* **and** use the **same** side *s*.  
Let `seg_{i}` and `seg_{j}` be the (identical) blocked segment for the two trains.  
Define auxiliary variables  

* `w_{i,j}^{τ}`  = `o_{i,j}·τ_{i,seg}`  
* `w_{j,i}^{τ}`  = `o_{i,j}·τ_{j,seg}`  

Linearisation (big‑M = `M_time`) :

```
w_{i,j}^{τ} ≤ M_time·o_{i,j}
w_{i,j}^{τ} ≥ 0
w_{i,j}^{τ} ≤ τ_{i,seg}
w_{i,j}^{τ} ≥ τ_{i,seg} – M_time·(1‑o_{i,j})
```

(and analogously for `w_{j,i}^{τ}`).

The **head‑way** constraint becomes

\[
a_{j,\text{entry}} \;\ge\; d_{i,\text{exit}} \;+\; safety\_gap\; o_{i,j}
\qquad\forall (i,j)\in P,\; \text{if } r_{i,s}=r_{j,s}=1
\tag{2}
\]

Because the model is linear, we replace the conditional “if both use the same side’’ by a big‑M formulation:

```
a_{j,entry} ≥ d_{i,exit} + safety_gap – M_ord·(2 – r_{i,s} – r_{j,s})
```

If either train does not use side *s*, the right‑hand side is relaxed by the big‑M term.

### 6.3  No conflict when opposite sides are used  

If two trains use opposite sides of the blocked segment they can occupy it simultaneously, therefore no ordering constraint is needed.  The big‑M term in (2) automatically de‑activates the constraint when `r_{i,s}+r_{j,s}=1`.

### 6.4  Dwell‑time at stations  

\[
d_{t,n}= a_{t,n}+ dwell_{n}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; n\in N_t
\tag{3}
\]

If a train is cancelled (`c_t = 1`) we relax the equality with a big‑M:

\[
d_{t,n} \ge a_{t,n}+ dwell_{n} - bigM_c\;c_t
\qquad
d_{t,n} \le a_{t,n}+ dwell_{n} + bigM_c\;c_t
\tag{3‑c}
\]

### 6.5  Travel‑time linking arrival / departure  

For every segment *seg* that train *t* traverses (including blocked and free segments):

\[
a_{t,\,\text{next}(n)} = d_{t,n} + \tau_{t,seg}
\qquad\forall t,\; n\in N_t\text{ with } seg = Seg(t,n)
\tag{4}
\]

If the train is cancelled we again relax with `bigM_c·c_t`.

### 6.6  Travel time ↔ speed (free segments)  

For any **free** segment *seg∈F* :

\[
\tau_{t,seg}= \frac{len_{seg}}{v_{t,seg}}
\qquad\forall t\text{ that use }seg
\tag{5}
\]

Because `v_{t,seg}` is a discrete speed, we enforce it with the `x`‑variables:

\[
v_{t,seg}= \sum_{\ell\in L} \hat v_{\ell}\,x_{t,seg,\ell}
\qquad\forall t,seg\in F
\tag{5‑a}
\]

\[
\sum_{\ell\in L} x_{t,seg,\ell}= 1 - c_t \qquad\forall t,seg\in F
\tag{5‑b}
\]

If the train is cancelled (`c_t=1`) the sum forces all `x` to 0 and consequently `v_{t,seg}=0`, `τ_{t,seg}=0`.

### 6.7  Speed limits (free segments)  

\[
v_{\min}\;(1-c_t) \le v_{t,seg} \le v_{\max}\;(1-c_t)
\qquad\forall t,seg\in F
\tag{6}
\]

### 6.8  Ordering‑consistency for each pair  

For every pair *(i,j)∈P* :

\[
o_{i,j}+o_{j,i}=1 \qquad\forall (i,j)\in P
\tag{7}
\]

If the two trains never share a segment (e.g. they are on different routes) we can set `o_{i,j}=0` a priori, but the above equality is safe because the big‑M in (2) will make the constraint non‑binding.

### 6.9  Blocked‑side occupation window  

No train may occupy the blocked side **s\*** (the side that is actually closed) during the disruption interval `[T_start,T_end]`.  
Let `s*` be the side that is **unavailable** (e.g. the left side). For any train *t* that uses the blocked segment:

\[
a_{t,\text{entry}} \ge T_{end} \; \text{or}\; d_{t,\text{exit}} \le T_{start}
\]

Linearised with a binary “use‑blocked‑side’’ variable `b_t = r_{t,s*}` :

```
a_{t,entry} ≥ T_end – M_time·(1‑b_t)
d_{t,exit} ≤ T_start + M_time·(1‑b_t)
```

If `b_t = 0` (train does **not** use the closed side) the constraints are relaxed; if `b_t = 1` they force the train to be completely outside the window.

### 6.10  Cancellation effect on delay term  

To keep the objective linear we set the delay contribution of a cancelled train to zero:

\[
a_{t,\text{last}} - \text{sched\_arr}_t \le M_{time}\;c_t
\qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{10}
\]

Thus when `c_t = 1` the term can be at most `M_time` (which is later subtracted by the weight, effectively removing the train from the objective).

### 6.11  Domain restrictions  

\[
\begin{aligned}
& r_{t,s}\in\{0,1\},\; o_{i,j}\in\{0,1\},\; c_t\in\{0,1\},\; x_{t,seg,\ell}\in\{0,1\}\\
& a_{t,n}\ge 0,\; d_{t,n}\ge 0,\; \tau_{t,seg}\ge 0,\; v_{t,seg}\ge 0,\; e_{t,seg}\ge 0
\end{aligned}
\tag{11}
\]

---

## 7.  Full MILP Model (compact notation)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& w_{\text{delay}}\sum_{t\in T}\bigl(a_{t,\text{last}}-\text{sched\_arr}_t\bigr)
      + w_{\text{energy}}\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{seg}\;e_{t,seg} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{s\in S} r_{t,s}=1 &&\forall t\text{ using a blocked segment} \tag{1}\\
& a_{j,\text{entry}} \ge d_{i,\text{exit}}+safety\_gap
   -M_{ord}\bigl(2-r_{i,s}-r_{j,s}\bigr) &&\forall (i,j)\in P,\;s\in S \tag{2}\\
& d_{t,n}=a_{t,n}+dwell_n &&\forall t,n \tag{3}\\
& a_{t,\text{next}(n)} = d_{t,n}+ \tau_{t,Seg(t,n)} &&\forall t,n \tag{4}\\
& \tau_{t,seg}= \frac{len_{seg}}{v_{t,seg}} &&\forall t,seg\in F \tag{5}\\
& v_{t,seg}= \sum_{\ell\in L}\hat v_{\ell}\,x_{t,seg,\ell} &&\forall t,seg\in F \tag{5a}\\
& \sum_{\ell\in L} x_{t,seg,\ell}=1-c_t &&\forall t,seg\in F \tag{5b}\\
& v_{\min}(1-c_t)\le v_{t,seg}\le v_{\max}(1-c_t) &&\forall t,seg\in F \tag{6}\\
& o_{i,j}+o_{j,i}=1 &&\forall (i,j)\in P \tag{7}\\
& a_{t,\text{entry}} \ge T_{end} - M_{time}(1-r_{t,s*}) &&\forall t \tag{8a}\\
& d_{t,\text{exit}} \le T_{start}+ M_{time}(1-r_{t,s*}) &&\forall t \tag{8b}\\
& a_{t,\text{last}}-\text{sched\_arr}_t \le M_{time}\,c_t &&\forall t \tag{10}\\
& \text{Linearisation constraints for } w_{i,j}^{\tau},\; w_{j,i}^{\tau},
   \; e_{t,seg}= \sum_{\ell} e_{\ell}\,x_{t,seg,\ell}\,\tau_{t,seg} \tag{Lin}\\
& \text{Domain restrictions } (11)
\end{aligned}
\]

All auxiliary linearisation constraints (labelled **Lin**) are the standard four‑inequality set described in Section 4.

---

## 8.  How the model works  

* **Side choice** – Constraint (1) forces each train that meets the blocked segment to pick exactly one side.  
* **Ordering** – If two trains pick the same side, binary `o_{i,j}` decides who goes first; (2) guarantees a safety head‑way. The big‑M term de‑activates the constraint when the trains are on opposite sides.  
* **Timing** – (3)–(4) propagate arrivals, departures and travel times along the whole route.  
* **Speed & energy** – The discrete speed level is selected by the `x`‑variables; (5)–(6) link speed to travel time and enforce limits. Energy consumption is linearised as the product of the chosen speed‑level rate and the travel time.  
* **Disruption window** – (8) forces any train that uses the *closed* side to be completely outside the interval `[T_start,T_end]`.  
* **Cancellation** – Binary `c_t` allows the model to drop a train (e.g. when the disruption makes it impossible to keep it on time). The big‑M terms in (3‑c), (4‑c) and (10) switch off all timing constraints and the delay contribution for cancelled trains.  
* **Objective** – A weighted sum of total passenger delay and total energy use is minimised. By adjusting `w_delay` and `w_energy` the planner can give priority to punctuality or to energy efficiency.

---

### Ready‑to‑use

The formulation above is **purely linear** (all products have been replaced by auxiliary variables and big‑M constraints).  It can be entered directly into any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …) using a modelling language such as AMPL, GAMS, Pyomo, or JuMP.  The only data that must be supplied are the sets, parameters (segment lengths, speed levels, dwell times, disruption window, etc.) and the big‑M constants that are large enough for the planning horizon.  

Feel free to adapt the weighting coefficients, tighten the big‑M values, or add extra practical constraints (e.g., crew‑change windows, platform capacity) – the structure of the model will remain unchanged.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

Below is a **complete linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** for the problem described in the prompt.  
The model integrates  

* **train‑rescheduling** (choice of which side of a partially blocked segment a train uses, and the order in which trains that share the same side pass the segment), and  
* **speed‑management** (selection of a discrete speed level on each free segment, which determines travel time and energy consumption).

All symbols, sets, parameters and decision variables are defined first, then the objective function, followed by a list of linear constraints.  Wherever a product of a binary variable and a continuous variable appears (e.g. `o_{i,j}·τ_{t,seg}`) a standard big‑M linearisation is used, so the whole model is a **MILP**.

---

## 1.  Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** | Set of trains, indexed by *t* |
| **S** | Set of sides of a blocked segment, `S = {L,R}` (left / right) |
| **B** | Set of **blocked** track segments (the segment that is partially closed) |
| **F** | Set of **free** track segments (all other segments) |
| **N_t** | Ordered set of stations visited by train *t* (including the entry and exit of every segment) |
| **Seg(t,n)** | Segment travelled by train *t* when it departs station *n* and arrives at the next station.  For a blocked segment the segment belongs to **B**, otherwise to **F**. |
| **P** | Set of ordered train pairs that share at least one common segment (i.e. could conflict).  Each element is a pair *(i,j)* with *i ≠ j*. |
| **L** | Set of admissible discrete speed levels, indexed by *ℓ* (e.g. ℓ = 1,…,L).  The actual speed value for level ℓ is `v̂_ℓ`. |

---

## 2.  Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Typical value / unit |
|--------|-------------|----------------------|
| `sched_arr_t` | Scheduled arrival time of train *t* at its final station (the “on‑time” reference) | minutes |
| `dwell_n` | Minimum dwell time at station *n* (same for all trains) | minutes |
| `len_seg` | Physical length of segment *seg* (km) | km |
| `v̂_ℓ` | Speed (km/min) associated with discrete level ℓ | km/min |
| `e_ℓ` | Energy consumption rate (kWh per minute) when travelling at speed level ℓ | kWh/min |
| `v_min , v_max` | Minimum / maximum admissible speed on any free segment (km/min) | km/min |
| `safety_gap` | Minimum temporal head‑way required between two trains on the same side (minutes) | minutes |
| `T_start , T_end` | Start / end of the disruption window during which the blocked side cannot be occupied (minutes) | minutes |
| `M_time` | A large enough time constant (big‑M) – e.g. the planning horizon (≥ max possible arrival time) | minutes |
| `M_ord` | A large enough ordering constant – e.g. `M_time` (used for ordering linearisation) | minutes |
| `w_delay` | Weight of total delay in the objective | – |
| `w_energy` | Weight of total energy consumption in the objective | – |
| `δ_{t,ℓ}` | Indicator: 1 if speed level ℓ is allowed for train *t* on a given segment (e.g. due to train‑type limits) | – |
| `bigM_c` | Large constant used to “turn off’’ a train when it is cancelled (≥ M_time) | minutes |

All big‑M constants are chosen **tight** but safely larger than any feasible value of the associated continuous variable (e.g. `M_time = planning horizon = 1440 min` for a 24‑h horizon).

---

## 3.  Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| `r_{t,s}` | binary | 1 if train *t* uses side *s* (L or R) of the blocked segment, 0 otherwise. |
| `o_{i,j}` | binary | 1 if train *i* passes the **shared** side **before** train *j* (i.e. *i* precedes *j*).  For any pair *(i,j)∈P* we also have `o_{j,i}=1‑o_{i,j}`. |
| `c_t` | binary | 1 if train *t* is **canceled** (i.e. removed from the schedule). |
| `a_{t,n}` | continuous ≥0 | Arrival time of train *t* at station *n*. |
| `d_{t,n}` | continuous ≥0 | Departure time of train *t* from station *n*. |
| `τ_{t,seg}` | continuous ≥0 | Travel time of train *t* on segment *seg*. |
| `x_{t,seg,ℓ}` | binary | 1 if train *t* travels on segment *seg* with speed level ℓ, 0 otherwise.  For each (t,seg) exactly one level is chosen (unless the train is cancelled). |
| `v_{t,seg}` | continuous ≥0 | Actual speed of train *t* on segment *seg* (km/min).  It will be forced to equal one of the discrete values `v̂_ℓ` through the `x`‑variables. |
| `e_{t,seg}` | continuous ≥0 | Energy consumption on segment *seg* (kWh).  Linearised as `e_{t,seg}= Σ_ℓ e_ℓ·x_{t,seg,ℓ}·τ_{t,seg}` (linearised with big‑M). |

---

## 4.  Linearisation of the product *binary × continuous*  

For any binary variable `z∈{0,1}` and continuous variable `y∈[0, Ymax]` we introduce an auxiliary continuous variable `w` that represents the product `z·y`:

```
w ≤  Ymax·z
w ≥  0
w ≤  y
w ≥  y – Ymax·(1‑z)
```

In the model we use this pattern for:

* `o_{i,j}·τ_{i,seg}` and `o_{i,j}·τ_{j,seg}` (ordering constraints) – with `Ymax = M_time`.
* `x_{t,seg,ℓ}·τ_{t,seg}` (energy term) – with `Ymax = M_time`.

All auxiliary variables are named `w_…` in the constraints below.

---

## 5.  Objective Function  

\[
\min \; 
\underbrace{w_{\text{delay}}\;\sum_{t\in T}\Bigl(a_{t,\text{last}}- \text{sched\_arr}_t\Bigr)}_{\text{total passenger delay}} 
\;+\;
\underbrace{w_{\text{energy}}\;\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{seg}\;e_{t,seg}}_{\text{total energy consumption}}
\]

*`a_{t,last}`* is the arrival time at the **final** station of train *t* (the last element of `N_t`).  
If a train is cancelled (`c_t = 1`) we force its contribution to the delay term to zero by adding a big‑M term (see constraint (13) below).

Both components are linear because `e_{t,seg}` has already been linearised.

---

## 6.  Constraints  

### 6.1  Side‑choice on the blocked segment  

For every train that traverses a blocked segment *b∈B* :

\[
\sum_{s\in S} r_{t,s}= 1 \qquad\forall t\in T\text{ that use }b
\tag{1}
\]

If a train does **not** use a blocked segment, the corresponding `r_{t,s}` variables are forced to 0 (or simply omitted).

### 6.2  Ordering on a common side  

Consider any ordered pair *(i,j)∈P* that share a **blocked** segment *b* **and** use the **same** side *s*.  
Let `seg_{i}` and `seg_{j}` be the (identical) blocked segment for the two trains.  
Define auxiliary variables  

* `w_{i,j}^{τ}`  = `o_{i,j}·τ_{i,seg}`  
* `w_{j,i}^{τ}`  = `o_{i,j}·τ_{j,seg}`  

Linearisation (big‑M = `M_time`) :

```
w_{i,j}^{τ} ≤ M_time·o_{i,j}
w_{i,j}^{τ} ≥ 0
w_{i,j}^{τ} ≤ τ_{i,seg}
w_{i,j}^{τ} ≥ τ_{i,seg} – M_time·(1‑o_{i,j})
```

(and analogously for `w_{j,i}^{τ}`).

The **head‑way** constraint becomes

\[
a_{j,\text{entry}} \;\ge\; d_{i,\text{exit}} \;+\; safety\_gap\; o_{i,j}
\qquad\forall (i,j)\in P,\; \text{if } r_{i,s}=r_{j,s}=1
\tag{2}
\]

Because the model is linear, we replace the conditional “if both use the same side’’ by a big‑M formulation:

```
a_{j,entry} ≥ d_{i,exit} + safety_gap – M_ord·(2 – r_{i,s} – r_{j,s})
```

If either train does not use side *s*, the right‑hand side is relaxed by the big‑M term.

### 6.3  No conflict when opposite sides are used  

If two trains use opposite sides of the blocked segment they can occupy it simultaneously, therefore no ordering constraint is needed.  The big‑M term in (2) automatically de‑activates the constraint when `r_{i,s}+r_{j,s}=1`.

### 6.4  Dwell‑time at stations  

\[
d_{t,n}= a_{t,n}+ dwell_{n}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; n\in N_t
\tag{3}
\]

If a train is cancelled (`c_t = 1`) we relax the equality with a big‑M:

\[
d_{t,n} \ge a_{t,n}+ dwell_{n} - bigM_c\;c_t
\qquad
d_{t,n} \le a_{t,n}+ dwell_{n} + bigM_c\;c_t
\tag{3‑c}
\]

### 6.5  Travel‑time linking arrival / departure  

For every segment *seg* that train *t* traverses (including blocked and free segments):

\[
a_{t,\,\text{next}(n)} = d_{t,n} + \tau_{t,seg}
\qquad\forall t,\; n\in N_t\text{ with } seg = Seg(t,n)
\tag{4}
\]

If the train is cancelled we again relax with `bigM_c·c_t`.

### 6.6  Travel time ↔ speed (free segments)  

For any **free** segment *seg∈F* :

\[
\tau_{t,seg}= \frac{len_{seg}}{v_{t,seg}}
\qquad\forall t\text{ that use }seg
\tag{5}
\]

Because `v_{t,seg}` is a discrete speed, we enforce it with the `x`‑variables:

\[
v_{t,seg}= \sum_{\ell\in L} \hat v_{\ell}\,x_{t,seg,\ell}
\qquad\forall t,seg\in F
\tag{5‑a}
\]

\[
\sum_{\ell\in L} x_{t,seg,\ell}= 1 - c_t \qquad\forall t,seg\in F
\tag{5‑b}
\]

If the train is cancelled (`c_t=1`) the sum forces all `x` to 0 and consequently `v_{t,seg}=0`, `τ_{t,seg}=0`.

### 6.7  Speed limits (free segments)  

\[
v_{\min}\;(1-c_t) \le v_{t,seg} \le v_{\max}\;(1-c_t)
\qquad\forall t,seg\in F
\tag{6}
\]

### 6.8  Ordering‑consistency for each pair  

For every pair *(i,j)∈P* :

\[
o_{i,j}+o_{j,i}=1 \qquad\forall (i,j)\in P
\tag{7}
\]

If the two trains never share a segment (e.g. they are on different routes) we can set `o_{i,j}=0` a priori, but the above equality is safe because the big‑M in (2) will make the constraint non‑binding.

### 6.9  Blocked‑side occupation window  

No train may occupy the blocked side **s\*** (the side that is actually closed) during the disruption interval `[T_start,T_end]`.  
Let `s*` be the side that is **unavailable** (e.g. the left side). For any train *t* that uses the blocked segment:

\[
a_{t,\text{entry}} \ge T_{end} \; \text{or}\; d_{t,\text{exit}} \le T_{start}
\]

Linearised with a binary “use‑blocked‑side’’ variable `b_t = r_{t,s*}` :

```
a_{t,entry} ≥ T_end – M_time·(1‑b_t)
d_{t,exit} ≤ T_start + M_time·(1‑b_t)
```

If `b_t = 0` (train does **not** use the closed side) the constraints are relaxed; if `b_t = 1` they force the train to be completely outside the window.

### 6.10  Cancellation effect on delay term  

To keep the objective linear we set the delay contribution of a cancelled train to zero:

\[
a_{t,\text{last}} - \text{sched\_arr}_t \le M_{time}\;c_t
\qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{10}
\]

Thus when `c_t = 1` the term can be at most `M_time` (which is later subtracted by the weight, effectively removing the train from the objective).

### 6.11  Domain restrictions  

\[
\begin{aligned}
& r_{t,s}\in\{0,1\},\; o_{i,j}\in\{0,1\},\; c_t\in\{0,1\},\; x_{t,seg,\ell}\in\{0,1\}\\
& a_{t,n}\ge 0,\; d_{t,n}\ge 0,\; \tau_{t,seg}\ge 0,\; v_{t,seg}\ge 0,\; e_{t,seg}\ge 0
\end{aligned}
\tag{11}
\]

---

## 7.  Full MILP Model (compact notation)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& w_{\text{delay}}\sum_{t\in T}\bigl(a_{t,\text{last}}-\text{sched\_arr}_t\bigr)
      + w_{\text{energy}}\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{seg}\;e_{t,seg} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{s\in S} r_{t,s}=1 &&\forall t\text{ using a blocked segment} \tag{1}\\
& a_{j,\text{entry}} \ge d_{i,\text{exit}}+safety\_gap
   -M_{ord}\bigl(2-r_{i,s}-r_{j,s}\bigr) &&\forall (i,j)\in P,\;s\in S \tag{2}\\
& d_{t,n}=a_{t,n}+dwell_n &&\forall t,n \tag{3}\\
& a_{t,\text{next}(n)} = d_{t,n}+ \tau_{t,Seg(t,n)} &&\forall t,n \tag{4}\\
& \tau_{t,seg}= \frac{len_{seg}}{v_{t,seg}} &&\forall t,seg\in F \tag{5}\\
& v_{t,seg}= \sum_{\ell\in L}\hat v_{\ell}\,x_{t,seg,\ell} &&\forall t,seg\in F \tag{5a}\\
& \sum_{\ell\in L} x_{t,seg,\ell}=1-c_t &&\forall t,seg\in F \tag{5b}\\
& v_{\min}(1-c_t)\le v_{t,seg}\le v_{\max}(1-c_t) &&\forall t,seg\in F \tag{6}\\
& o_{i,j}+o_{j,i}=1 &&\forall (i,j)\in P \tag{7}\\
& a_{t,\text{entry}} \ge T_{end} - M_{time}(1-r_{t,s*}) &&\forall t \tag{8a}\\
& d_{t,\text{exit}} \le T_{start}+ M_{time}(1-r_{t,s*}) &&\forall t \tag{8b}\\
& a_{t,\text{last}}-\text{sched\_arr}_t \le M_{time}\,c_t &&\forall t \tag{10}\\
& \text{Linearisation constraints for } w_{i,j}^{\tau},\; w_{j,i}^{\tau},
   \; e_{t,seg}= \sum_{\ell} e_{\ell}\,x_{t,seg,\ell}\,\tau_{t,seg} \tag{Lin}\\
& \text{Domain restrictions } (11)
\end{aligned}
\]

All auxiliary linearisation constraints (labelled **Lin**) are the standard four‑inequality set described in Section 4.

---

## 8.  How the model works  

* **Side choice** – Constraint (1) forces each train that meets the blocked segment to pick exactly one side.  
* **Ordering** – If two trains pick the same side, binary `o_{i,j}` decides who goes first; (2) guarantees a safety head‑way. The big‑M term de‑activates the constraint when the trains are on opposite sides.  
* **Timing** – (3)–(4) propagate arrivals, departures and travel times along the whole route.  
* **Speed & energy** – The discrete speed level is selected by the `x`‑variables; (5)–(6) link speed to travel time and enforce limits. Energy consumption is linearised as the product of the chosen speed‑level rate and the travel time.  
* **Disruption window** – (8) forces any train that uses the *closed* side to be completely outside the interval `[T_start,T_end]`.  
* **Cancellation** – Binary `c_t` allows the model to drop a train (e.g. when the disruption makes it impossible to keep it on time). The big‑M terms in (3‑c), (4‑c) and (10) switch off all timing constraints and the delay contribution for cancelled trains.  
* **Objective** – A weighted sum of total passenger delay and total energy use is minimised. By adjusting `w_delay` and `w_energy` the planner can give priority to punctuality or to energy efficiency.

---

### Ready‑to‑use

The formulation above is **purely linear** (all products have been replaced by auxiliary variables and big‑M constraints).  It can be entered directly into any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …) using a modelling language such as AMPL, GAMS, Pyomo, or JuMP.  The only data that must be supplied are the sets, parameters (segment lengths, speed levels, dwell times, disruption window, etc.) and the big‑M constants that are large enough for the planning horizon.  

Feel free to adapt the weighting coefficients, tighten the big‑M values, or add extra practical constraints (e.g., crew‑change windows, platform capacity) – the structure of the model will remain unchanged.

response.content:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)**  

---

### 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** | Set of trains, indexed by *t* |
| **S** = {L,R} | Two sides of a partially blocked segment (Left / Right) |
| **B** | Set of *blocked* track segments (the segment that suffers a partial blockage) |
| **F** | Set of *free* track segments (all other segments) |
| **Nₜ** | Ordered set of stations visited by train *t* (including entry/exit of every segment) |
| **Seg(t,n)** | Segment travelled by train *t* when it departs station *n* and arrives at the next station |
| **P** | Set of ordered train pairs *(i,j)* that share at least one common segment (potential conflict) |
| **L** | Set of admissible discrete speed levels, indexed by ℓ (ℓ = 1,…,|L|) |

---

### 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Typical value / unit |
|--------|-------------|----------------------|
| `sched_arrₜ` | Scheduled arrival time of train *t* at its final station (reference “on‑time’’) | minutes |
| `dwellₙ` | Minimum dwell time at station *n* (same for all trains) | minutes |
| `len_seg` | Physical length of segment *seg* | km |
| `v̂_ℓ` | Speed (km / min) associated with speed level ℓ | km / min |
| `e_ℓ` | Energy consumption rate (kWh / min) when travelling at speed level ℓ | kWh / min |
| `v_min , v_max` | Minimum / maximum admissible speed on any free segment | km / min |
| `safety_gap` | Minimum temporal head‑way required between two trains on the same side | minutes |
| `T_start , T_end` | Start / end of the disruption window (the side that is closed cannot be occupied) | minutes |
| `M_time` | Large constant ≥ planning horizon (e.g. 1440 min) | minutes |
| `M_ord` | Large constant for ordering linearisation (≥ M_time) | minutes |
| `bigM_c` | Large constant for cancellation (≥ M_time) | minutes |
| `w_delay` | Weight of total delay in the objective | – |
| `w_energy` | Weight of total energy consumption in the objective | – |
| `δₜ,ℓ` | 1 if speed level ℓ is allowed for train *t* (otherwise 0) | – |

---

### 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| `rₜₛ` ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 ⇔ train *t* uses side *s* of the blocked segment |
| `oᵢⱼ` ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* passes the shared side **before** train *j* |
| `cₜ` ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 ⇔ train *t* is cancelled |
| `aₜₙ` ≥ 0 | continuous | Arrival time of train *t* at station *n* |
| `dₜₙ` ≥ 0 | continuous | Departure time of train *t* from station *n* |
| `τₜₛₑg` ≥ 0 | continuous | Travel time of train *t* on segment *seg* |
| `xₜₛₑgℓ` ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 ⇔ train *t* travels on segment *seg* with speed level ℓ |
| `vₜₛₑg` ≥ 0 | continuous | Actual speed of train *t* on segment *seg* |
| `eₜₛₑg` ≥ 0 | continuous | Energy consumption of train *t* on segment *seg* |
| `wᵢⱼᵗ` ≥ 0 | continuous | Auxiliary variable for product `oᵢⱼ·τᵢₛₑg` (linearisation) |
| `w'ᵢⱼᵗ` ≥ 0 | continuous | Auxiliary variable for product `oᵢⱼ·τⱼₛₑg` (linearisation) |
| `zₜₛₑgℓ` ≥ 0 | continuous | Auxiliary variable for product `xₜₛₑgℓ·τₜₛₑg` (energy linearisation) |

---

### 4. Linearisation of binary × continuous products  

For any binary `y∈{0,1}` and continuous `u∈[0,U]` introduce `p = y·u` and enforce  

```
p ≤ U·y
p ≥ 0
p ≤ u
p ≥ u – U·(1‑y)
```

All auxiliary variables (`wᵢⱼᵗ`, `w'ᵢⱼᵗ`, `zₜₛₑgℓ`) are defined with `U = M_time`.

---

### 5. Objective Function  

\[
\min\;
w_{\text{delay}}\;\sum_{t\in T}\bigl(a_{t,\text{last}}-\text{sched\_arr}_t\bigr)
\;+\;
w_{\text{energy}}\;\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{seg\in B\cup F} e_{t,seg}
\]

`a_{t,last}` is the arrival time at the final station of train *t*.  
If a train is cancelled (`cₜ=1`) its delay contribution is forced to zero by constraint (10) below.

---

### 6. Constraints  

#### 6.1  Side choice (blocked segment)  
\[
\sum_{s\in S} r_{t,s}=1 \qquad\forall t\text{ that traverse a blocked segment }b\in B \tag{1}
\]

#### 6.2  Ordering on a common side (conflict avoidance)  

For every pair *(i,j)∈P* that share a blocked segment *b* and **use the same side** *s*:  

```
a_{j,entry} ≥ d_{i,exit} + safety_gap – M_ord·(2 – r_{i,s} – r_{j,s})      (2)
```

If either train does not use side *s*, the big‑M term relaxes the constraint.

#### 6.3  Dwell time at stations  

\[
d_{t,n}=a_{t,n}+dwell_{n}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; n\in N_t \tag{3}
\]

If train *t* is cancelled, relax with `bigM_c·cₜ` (both lower and upper bound).

#### 6.4  Propagation of arrival–departure through a segment  

\[
a_{t,\text{next}(n)} = d_{t,n}+ \tau_{t,Seg(t,n)} \qquad\forall t,\; n\in N_t \tag{4}
\]

Again, relax with `bigM_c·cₜ` when `cₜ=1`.

#### 6.5  Travel‑time ↔ speed (free segments)  

\[
\tau_{t,seg}= \frac{len_{seg}}{v_{t,seg}} \qquad\forall t,\; seg\in F \tag{5}
\]

Speed discretisation:  

\[
v_{t,seg}= \sum_{\ell\in L}\hat v_{\ell}\,x_{t,seg,\ell} \qquad\forall t,\; seg\in F \tag{5a}
\]

Exactly one speed level (or none if cancelled):  

\[
\sum_{\ell\in L} x_{t,seg,\ell}= 1-c_{t} \qquad\forall t,\; seg\in F \tag{5b}
\]

Speed limits:  

\[
v_{\min}(1-c_{t}) \le v_{t,seg} \le v_{\max}(1-c_{t}) \qquad\forall t,\; seg\in F \tag{6}
\]

#### 6.6  Ordering consistency  

\[
o_{i,j}+o_{j,i}=1 \qquad\forall (i,j)\in P \tag{7}
\]

#### 6.7  Blocked‑side occupation window  

Let `s*` be the side that is **closed** during the disruption. For any train that uses the blocked segment:

```
a_{t,entry} ≥ T_end – M_time·(1 – r_{t,s*})          (8a)
d_{t,exit}  ≤ T_start + M_time·(1 – r_{t,s*})          (8b)
```

If `r_{t,s*}=0` the constraints are relaxed; if `r_{t,s*}=1` the train must be completely outside the window.

#### 6.8  Energy linearisation  

Energy on a segment is the product of the chosen speed‑level rate and travel time:

\[
e_{t,seg}= \sum_{\ell\in L} e_{\ell}\,z_{t,seg,\ell} \qquad\forall t,seg
\]

with auxiliary `z_{t,seg,\ell}` defined by the binary‑continuous linearisation (U = M_time) applied to `x_{t,seg,\ell}·τ_{t,seg}`.

#### 6.9  Cancellation effect on delay term  

\[
a_{t,\text{last}}-\text{sched\_arr}_t \le M_time\;c_{t} \qquad\forall t\in T \tag{10}
\]

Thus a cancelled train contributes at most a constant that can be ignored by the objective.

#### 6.10  Linearisation auxiliary constraints  

For each `(i,j,seg)` needed in (2) introduce `wᵢⱼᵗ` and `w'ᵢⱼᵗ`:

```
wᵢⱼᵗ ≤ M_time·oᵢⱼ
wᵢⱼᵗ ≥ 0
wᵢⱼᵗ ≤ τᵢ,seg
wᵢⱼᵗ ≥ τᵢ,seg – M_time·(1‑oᵢⱼ)
```

Analogous for `w'ᵢⱼᵗ` with τⱼ,seg.  

For each `(t,seg,ℓ)` introduce `z_{t,seg,ℓ}`:

```
z_{t,seg,ℓ} ≤ M_time·x_{t,seg,ℓ}
z_{t,seg,ℓ} ≥ 0
z_{t,seg,ℓ} ≤ τ_{t,seg}
z_{t,seg,ℓ} ≥ τ_{t,seg} – M_time·(1‑x_{t,seg,ℓ})
```

#### 6.11  Domain restrictions  

\[
\begin{aligned}
& r_{t,s},\; o_{i,j},\; c_t,\; x_{t,seg,\ell}\in\{0,1\}\\
& a_{t,n},\; d_{t,n},\; \tau_{t,seg},\; v_{t,seg},\; e_{t,seg},\; w^{\cdot},\; z^{\cdot}\ge 0
\end{aligned}
\tag{11}
\]

---

### 7. Full MILP (compact form)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& w_{\text{delay}}\sum_{t\in T}\bigl(a_{t,\text{last}}-\text{sched\_arr}_t\bigr)
      + w_{\text{energy}}\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{seg} e_{t,seg}\\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{s\in S} r_{t,s}=1 &&\forall t\text{ using a blocked segment} \tag{1}\\
& a_{j,entry}\ge d_{i,exit}+safety\_gap-M_{ord}(2-r_{i,s}-r_{j,s}) &&\forall (i,j)\in P,\;s\in S \tag{2}\\
& d_{t,n}=a_{t,n}+dwell_n &&\forall t,n \tag{3}\\
& a_{t,next(n)} = d_{t,n}+ \tau_{t,Seg(t,n)} &&\forall t,n \tag{4}\\
& \tau_{t,seg}= \frac{len_{seg}}{v_{t,seg}} &&\forall t,seg\in F \tag{5}\\
& v_{t,seg}= \sum_{\ell\in L}\hat v_{\ell}x_{t,seg,\ell} &&\forall t,seg\in F \tag{5a}\\
& \sum_{\ell\in L}x_{t,seg,\ell}=1-c_t &&\forall t,seg\in F \tag{5b}\\
& v_{\min}(1-c_t)\le v_{t,seg}\le v_{\max}(1-c_t) &&\forall t,seg\in F \tag{6}\\
& o_{i,j}+o_{j,i}=1 &&\forall (i,j)\in P \tag{7}\\
& a_{t,entry}\ge T_{end}-M_{time}(1-r_{t,s*}) &&\forall t \tag{8a}\\
& d_{t,exit}\le T_{start}+M_{time}(1-r_{t,s*}) &&\forall t \tag{8b}\\
& e_{t,seg}= \sum_{\ell\in L} e_{\ell}z_{t,seg,\ell} &&\forall t,seg \tag{9}\\
& a_{t,last}-\text{sched\_arr}_t \le M_{time}c_t &&\forall t \tag{10}\\
& \text{Binary–continuous linearisation constraints (w, w', z)} \tag{Lin}\\
& \text{Domain restrictions (11)} 
\end{aligned}
\]

All products have been replaced by the auxiliary variables defined in Section 4, so the model is a **mixed‑integer linear program**.

---

### 8. How to use  

*Supply* the sets, parameters (segment lengths, speed levels, dwell times, disruption window, big‑M values) and the weighting coefficients `w_delay`, `w_energy`.  
*Load* the model into any MILP solver (Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, SCIP, …) via a modelling language (Pyomo, JuMP, AMPL, GAMS).  
The solver will return:

* side choice `rₜₛ` (which side of the blocked segment each train uses),  
* ordering `oᵢⱼ` (who passes first on a shared side),  
* feasible arrival/departure times `aₜₙ`, `dₜₙ`,  
* selected speed levels `xₜₛₑgℓ` (hence speeds `vₜₛₑg` and travel times `τₜₛₑg`),  
* and the total delay and energy consumption.

The model simultaneously guarantees a **conflict‑free timetable**, **executable speed profiles**, and **energy‑efficient** operation under a partial‑segment blockage. Adjusting the weights allows the planner to prioritize punctuality or energy savings, and the optional cancellation variables enable the model to drop trains when recovery is impossible.

| `dₜₙ` ≥ 0 | continuous | Departure time of train *t* from station *n* |
| `τₜₛₑg` ≥ 0 | continuous | Travel time of train *t* on segment *seg* |
| `xₜₛₑgℓ` ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 ⇔ train *t* travels on segment *seg* with speed level ℓ |
| `vₜₛₑg` ≥ 0 | continuous | Actual speed of train *t* on segment *seg* |
| `eₜₛₑg` ≥ 0 | continuous | Energy consumption of train *t* on segment *seg* |
| `wᵢⱼᵗ` ≥ 0 | continuous | Auxiliary variable for product `oᵢⱼ·τᵢₛₑg` (linearisation) |
| `w'ᵢⱼᵗ` ≥ 0 | continuous | Auxiliary variable for product `oᵢⱼ·τⱼₛₑg` (linearisation) |
| `zₜₛₑgℓ` ≥ 0 | continuous | Auxiliary variable for product `xₜₛₑgℓ·τₜₛₑg` (energy linearisation) |

---

### 4. Linearisation of binary × continuous products  

For any binary `y∈{0,1}` and continuous `u∈[0,U]` introduce `p = y·u` and enforce  

```
p ≤ U·y
p ≥ 0
p ≤ u
p ≥ u – U·(1‑y)
```

All auxiliary variables (`wᵢⱼᵗ`, `w'ᵢⱼᵗ`, `zₜₛₑgℓ`) are defined with `U = M_time`.

---

### 5. Objective Function  

\[
\min\;
w_{\text{delay}}\;\sum_{t\in T}\bigl(a_{t,\text{last}}-\text{sched\_arr}_t\bigr)
\;+\;
w_{\text{energy}}\;\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{seg\in B\cup F} e_{t,seg}
\]

`a_{t,last}` is the arrival time at the final station of train *t*.  
If a train is cancelled (`cₜ=1`) its delay contribution is forced to zero by constraint (10) below.

---

### 6. Constraints  

#### 6.1  Side choice (blocked segment)  
\[
\sum_{s\in S} r_{t,s}=1 \qquad\forall t\text{ that traverse a blocked segment }b\in B \tag{1}
\]

#### 6.2  Ordering on a common side (conflict avoidance)  

For every pair *(i,j)∈P* that share a blocked segment *b* and **use the same side** *s*:  

```
a_{j,entry} ≥ d_{i,exit} + safety_gap – M_ord·(2 – r_{i,s} – r_{j,s})      (2)
```

If either train does not use side *s*, the big‑M term relaxes the constraint.

#### 6.3  Dwell time at stations  

\[
d_{t,n}=a_{t,n}+dwell_{n}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; n\in N_t \tag{3}
\]

If train *t* is cancelled, relax with `bigM_c·cₜ` (both lower and upper bound).

#### 6.4  Propagation of arrival–departure through a segment  

\[
a_{t,\text{next}(n)} = d_{t,n}+ \tau_{t,Seg(t,n)} \qquad\forall t,\; n\in N_t \tag{4}
\]

Again, relax with `bigM_c·cₜ` when `cₜ=1`.

#### 6.5  Travel‑time ↔ speed (free segments)  

\[
\tau_{t,seg}= \frac{len_{seg}}{v_{t,seg}} \qquad\forall t,\; seg\in F \tag{5}
\]

Speed discretisation:  

\[
v_{t,seg}= \sum_{\ell\in L}\hat v_{\ell}\,x_{t,seg,\ell} \qquad\forall t,\; seg\in F \tag{5a}
\]

Exactly one speed level (or none if cancelled):  

\[
\sum_{\ell\in L} x_{t,seg,\ell}= 1-c_{t} \qquad\forall t,\; seg\in F \tag{5b}
\]

Speed limits:  

\[
v_{\min}(1-c_{t}) \le v_{t,seg} \le v_{\max}(1-c_{t}) \qquad\forall t,\; seg\in F \tag{6}
\]

#### 6.6  Ordering consistency  

\[
o_{i,j}+o_{j,i}=1 \qquad\forall (i,j)\in P \tag{7}
\]

#### 6.7  Blocked‑side occupation window  

Let `s*` be the side that is **closed** during the disruption. For any train that uses the blocked segment:

```
a_{t,entry} ≥ T_end – M_time·(1 – r_{t,s*})          (8a)
d_{t,exit}  ≤ T_start + M_time·(1 – r_{t,s*})          (8b)
```

If `r_{t,s*}=0` the constraints are relaxed; if `r_{t,s*}=1` the train must be completely outside the window.

#### 6.8  Energy linearisation  

Energy on a segment is the product of the chosen speed‑level rate and travel time:

\[
e_{t,seg}= \sum_{\ell\in L} e_{\ell}\,z_{t,seg,\ell} \qquad\forall t,seg
\]

with auxiliary `z_{t,seg,\ell}` defined by the binary‑continuous linearisation (U = M_time) applied to `x_{t,seg,\ell}·τ_{t,seg}`.

#### 6.9  Cancellation effect on delay term  

\[
a_{t,\text{last}}-\text{sched\_arr}_t \le M_time\;c_{t} \qquad\forall t\in T \tag{10}
\]

Thus a cancelled train contributes at most a constant that can be ignored by the objective.

#### 6.10  Linearisation auxiliary constraints  

For each `(i,j,seg)` needed in (2) introduce `wᵢⱼᵗ` and `w'ᵢⱼᵗ`:

```
wᵢⱼᵗ ≤ M_time·oᵢⱼ
wᵢⱼᵗ ≥ 0
wᵢⱼᵗ ≤ τᵢ,seg
wᵢⱼᵗ ≥ τᵢ,seg – M_time·(1‑oᵢⱼ)
```

Analogous for `w'ᵢⱼᵗ` with τⱼ,seg.  

For each `(t,seg,ℓ)` introduce `z_{t,seg,ℓ}`:

```
z_{t,seg,ℓ} ≤ M_time·x_{t,seg,ℓ}
z_{t,seg,ℓ} ≥ 0
z_{t,seg,ℓ} ≤ τ_{t,seg}
z_{t,seg,ℓ} ≥ τ_{t,seg} – M_time·(1‑x_{t,seg,ℓ})
```

#### 6.11  Domain restrictions  

\[
\begin{aligned}
& r_{t,s},\; o_{i,j},\; c_t,\; x_{t,seg,\ell}\in\{0,1\}\\
& a_{t,n},\; d_{t,n},\; \tau_{t,seg},\; v_{t,seg},\; e_{t,seg},\; w^{\cdot},\; z^{\cdot}\ge 0
\end{aligned}
\tag{11}
\]

---

### 7. Full MILP (compact form)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& w_{\text{delay}}\sum_{t\in T}\bigl(a_{t,\text{last}}-\text{sched\_arr}_t\bigr)
      + w_{\text{energy}}\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{seg} e_{t,seg}\\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{s\in S} r_{t,s}=1 &&\forall t\text{ using a blocked segment} \tag{1}\\
& a_{j,entry}\ge d_{i,exit}+safety\_gap-M_{ord}(2-r_{i,s}-r_{j,s}) &&\forall (i,j)\in P,\;s\in S \tag{2}\\
& d_{t,n}=a_{t,n}+dwell_n &&\forall t,n \tag{3}\\
& a_{t,next(n)} = d_{t,n}+ \tau_{t,Seg(t,n)} &&\forall t,n \tag{4}\\
& \tau_{t,seg}= \frac{len_{seg}}{v_{t,seg}} &&\forall t,seg\in F \tag{5}\\
& v_{t,seg}= \sum_{\ell\in L}\hat v_{\ell}x_{t,seg,\ell} &&\forall t,seg\in F \tag{5a}\\
& \sum_{\ell\in L}x_{t,seg,\ell}=1-c_t &&\forall t,seg\in F \tag{5b}\\
& v_{\min}(1-c_t)\le v_{t,seg}\le v_{\max}(1-c_t) &&\forall t,seg\in F \tag{6}\\
& o_{i,j}+o_{j,i}=1 &&\forall (i,j)\in P \tag{7}\\
& a_{t,entry}\ge T_{end}-M_{time}(1-r_{t,s*}) &&\forall t \tag{8a}\\
& d_{t,exit}\le T_{start}+M_{time}(1-r_{t,s*}) &&\forall t \tag{8b}\\
& e_{t,seg}= \sum_{\ell\in L} e_{\ell}z_{t,seg,\ell} &&\forall t,seg \tag{9}\\
& a_{t,last}-\text{sched\_arr}_t \le M_{time}c_t &&\forall t \tag{10}\\
& \text{Binary–continuous linearisation constraints (w, w', z)} \tag{Lin}\\
& \text{Domain restrictions (11)} 
\end{aligned}
\]

All products have been replaced by the auxiliary variables defined in Section 4, so the model is a **mixed‑integer linear program**.

---

### 8. How to use  

*Supply* the sets, parameters (segment lengths, speed levels, dwell times, disruption window, big‑M values) and the weighting coefficients `w_delay`, `w_energy`.  
*Load* the model into any MILP solver (Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, SCIP, …) via a modelling language (Pyomo, JuMP, AMPL, GAMS).  
The solver will return:

* side choice `rₜₛ` (which side of the blocked segment each train uses),  
* ordering `oᵢⱼ` (who passes first on a shared side),  
* feasible arrival/departure times `aₜₙ`, `dₜₙ`,  
* selected speed levels `xₜₛₑgℓ` (hence speeds `vₜₛₑg` and travel times `τₜₛₑg`),  
* and the total delay and energy consumption.

The model simultaneously guarantees a **conflict‑free timetable**, **executable speed profiles**, and **energy‑efficient** operation under a partial‑segment blockage. Adjusting the weights allows the planner to prioritize punctuality or energy savings, and the optional cancellation variables enable the model to drop trains when recovery is impossible.
